items.title: File permissions
items.context: Each file has read (4), write (2) and execute (1) bits for owner, group and others. chmod 754 means owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others r-- (4). On a directory, x means 'may enter/traverse'.

questions.prompt: What does chmod 640 secret.txt allow?
choices: Owner everything, group read, others read
Owner read, group read+write, others nothing
Everyone can read; only the owner can write
Owner read+write, group read, others nothing

items.title: Signals
items.context: kill sends SIGTERM (15) by default: a polite request the process can catch to shut down cleanly. SIGKILL (9) can't be caught, blocked or ignored — the kernel just ends the process, with no cleanup. SIGHUP is often used to make daemons reload config.

questions.prompt: Which signal can a process NOT catch or ignore?
questions.explanation: That's why kill -9 is a last resort: no flushing buffers, no removing lock files.

questions.prompt: What's the right way to stop a service so it can finish in-flight work?
choices: Send SIGTERM, wait a grace period, then SIGKILL if it's still running
questions.explanation: Docker and Kubernetes do exactly this: SIGTERM, a grace period (10 s / 30 s by default), then SIGKILL.

items.title: systemd units
items.context: systemctl start runs a unit now; systemctl enable makes it start at boot (it creates the symlinks), without starting it now — use enable --now for both. journalctl -u nginx -f follows that unit's logs.

questions.prompt: After systemctl enable nginx (and nothing else), nginx is:
choices: Set to start at boot, but not necessarily running now
Running now and at every boot
Running now, but won't start at boot
questions.explanation: enable configures boot behaviour only; enable --now also starts it.

items.title: Redirection
items.context: > redirects stdout, 2> stderr, and 2>&1 points stderr wherever stdout points at that moment, so order matters: cmd > out.log 2>&1 sends both to the file, but cmd 2>&1 > out.log sends stderr to the terminal and only stdout to the file.

questions.prompt: Where does stderr go with: ./job.sh 2>&1 > out.log ?
choices: The terminal — stderr was duplicated before stdout moved to the file
questions.explanation: Redirections are applied left to right. Write cmd > out.log 2>&1 to capture both.

items.title: Safer shell scripts
items.context: set -e exits on the first failing command, set -u treats unset variables as errors, and set -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any command in it fails (not just the last one). Exit code 0 means success; anything else is failure.

questions.prompt: What does set -o pipefail change?
choices: A pipeline's exit status is that of the last command that failed, so a failure anywhere is caught
questions.explanation: Without it, curl ... | jq . 'succeeds' as long as jq succeeds, even if curl failed.

items.title: Disk space mysteries
items.context: df reports filesystem usage; du sums the files it can see. If df says the disk is full but du finds far less, a deleted file is usually still held open by a running process (often a log file). lsof +L1 lists open-but-deleted files; restarting or signalling the process frees the space.

questions.prompt: df shows / at 100%, but du -sh / finds 30% less. The likely cause is:
choices: A deleted file still held open by a process
questions.explanation: The inode lives until the last open handle closes. Truncating with > file instead of rm avoids this for live logs.

items.title: Listening ports
items.context: ss -tlnp (or the older netstat -tlnp) lists listening TCP sockets with the owning process. -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric (no DNS lookups), -p show process.

questions.prompt: Which command shows which process is listening on port 8080?
questions.explanation: Then grep for :8080; lsof -i :8080 works too.

items.title: Environment variables
items.context: VAR=value sets a shell variable; export VAR makes it part of the environment that child processes inherit. A script run as ./script.sh gets a copy and can't change the parent shell's variables; source script.sh runs it in the current shell.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't ./set-env.sh change variables in your current terminal?
choices: It runs in a child process; changes don't propagate back to the parent
questions.explanation: Use source set-env.sh (or . set-env.sh) to run it in the current shell.

items.title: Cron schedules
items.context: A crontab line has five time fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, then the command. */15 in the minute field means every 15 minutes; day-of-week 0 or 7 is Sunday.

questions.prompt: When does 0 2 * * 1 /backup.sh run?
choices: At 00:02 on the 1st of each month
questions.explanation: minute=0, hour=2, any day of month, any month, day-of-week=1 (Monday).

items.title: Hard vs symbolic links
items.context: A hard link is another name for the same inode: it survives deleting the original name but can't cross filesystems or point at directories. A symbolic link stores a path; it can cross filesystems but breaks (dangles) if the target is removed.

questions.prompt: You delete the original file. Which link still shows the content?
questions.explanation: The data stays until the last hard link is removed; a symlink just points at a path that no longer exists.

items.title: Text tools
items.context: grep finds lines, awk splits lines into fields ($1, $2…), sed edits streams (s/old/new/). They compose with pipes: grep ERROR app.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c.

questions.prompt: What does echo "alpha beta gamma" | awk '{print $2}' print?
questions.explanation: awk splits on whitespace by default; $2 is the second field.

items.title: find
items.context: find searches by name, type, size and time: find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime +7 matches .log files last modified more than 7 days ago; adding -delete removes them. Run it without -delete first.

questions.prompt: find /var/log -name "*.gz" -mtime +30 -delete removes:
choices: Logs created in the last 30 days
Compressed logs not modified for more than 30 days
questions.explanation: -mtime +30 means modified more than 30 × 24 h ago.

items.title: Load average
items.context: uptime and top show the 1-, 5- and 15-minute load averages: the average number of tasks running or waiting (on Linux, including uninterruptible I/O waits). Compare it with the CPU count: a load of 4.0 on 4 cores means fully busy; 8.0 means work is queuing.

questions.prompt: A 2-core VM has a sustained load average of 6. That means:
choices: Work is queuing — demand is about 3× the capacity
questions.explanation: Check whether it's CPU-bound (top %CPU) or stuck on I/O (wa, iostat).

items.title: sudo
items.context: sudo runs a command as another user (root by default) according to /etc/sudoers. Always edit that file with visudo, which checks the syntax first — a broken sudoers file can lock you out of root.

questions.prompt: How should you edit /etc/sudoers?
questions.explanation: visudo locks the file and refuses to save invalid syntax.

items.title: SSH keys
items.context: With key authentication, the server stores your public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; the private key never leaves your machine (protect it with a passphrase or agent). Disable password login on servers once keys work.

questions.prompt: Which key do you copy to the server?
questions.explanation: ssh-copy-id user@host does it for you.

items.title: Archives
items.context: tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/ creates (c) a gzip-compressed (z) archive file (f). tar -xzf backup.tar.gz extracts (x) it; -t lists the contents.

questions.prompt: Which command extracts backup.tar.gz?
questions.explanation: c = create, x = extract, t = list.

items.title: Inspecting HTTP with curl
items.context: curl -I fetches only the response headers; curl -v shows the whole exchange including TLS and request headers; curl -L follows redirects; curl -s silences progress output for scripts.

questions.prompt: You want to check an endpoint's status code and headers only. Use:
questions.explanation: -I sends a HEAD request.

items.title: Package managers
items.context: Debian and Ubuntu use apt (.deb packages); RHEL, Rocky and Fedora use dnf (formerly yum, .rpm packages); Alpine uses apk. Container images often use Alpine (apk) or Debian-slim (apt).

questions.prompt: Installing curl on a Rocky Linux server:
questions.explanation: Rocky is RHEL-compatible, so it uses dnf.

items.title: Memory: free vs available
items.context: Linux uses spare RAM as page cache, so the 'free' column in free -h is usually small. 'available' estimates how much memory new work can get, including reclaimable cache. Low 'free' alone isn't a problem; low 'available' plus swapping is.

questions.prompt: free -h shows 200 MB free but 6 GB available. The server is:
choices: Fine — most memory is reclaimable cache
About to run out of memory
questions.explanation: The kernel gives cache back when applications need it.
